paragraphs.source_en: From the mid-sixteenth century, the central administration attempted to limit the power of the military elite. But rather than reduce the role of the cavalry or reorganise the Janissary infantry—particularly to reduce the expense of maintaining the latter—the administration began to hire additional salaried troops in the provinces from among commoners. These foot soldiers armed with muskets were used by commanders in imperial Being Ottoman, Being Roman 249 campaigns against the Habsburgs and the Safavids. The armies of Christian Europe especially had seen benefit in equipping their infantry with the latest types of firearms.*° The diffusion of firearms had lasting societal effects in the Ottoman Empire. Whether they deserted or returned from a usually unsuccessful military campaign, provincial foot soldiers kept their weapons.

paragraphs.source_en: At the same time, provincial governors in Anatolia and the Arabic-speaking regions enlisted musketeers as mercenaries for their private arrnies. These men terrorised the countryside as bands of outlaws.*! Anatolia and Syria were rent by rebellion and brigandry for decades. International commerce and money changing caused cash to flow into the empire, which allowed rebel leaders who engaged in these new sources of wealth, like imperial army commanders and regional governors, to hire mercenaries equipped with firearms.” These rebels had made great fortunes and were able to use their wealth to buy their way into political power, bribing their way into office.** They were more like rogue clients who wanted their piece of the pie. Some demanded to join the professional army of the Janissaries and enter the military class, which meant becoming Ottomans.
